opus-5.5.text:
I think it's going to shift a lot, and probably in a direction people at the labs don't fully appreciate yet.

Right now there's this weird moment where a few hundred, maybe a few thousand, people at a handful of labs have enormous influence over the trajectory of the most important technology in the world. Employees have real leverage. We saw it during the OpenAI board episode: when basically the whole company threatened to walk, that decided the outcome. Talent is the scarce resource. If the key researchers leave, the lab's roadmap leaves with them. So employees can shape safety policy, what gets deployed, who the lab partners with, just by voting with their feet.

But I think that leverage is temporary, for two reasons.

The first is automation. The whole thesis is that we're heading toward automated AI research. Once you can run millions of copies of an automated AI researcher, the marginal human researcher matters much less. Their leverage came from being the bottleneck. When they stop being the bottleneck, the power moves to whoever controls the compute and the model weights. That's leadership, and increasingly, whoever is backing the compute buildout.

The second, and bigger, is the government. As it becomes clear this is a decisive national security technology, superintelligence as the thing that determines military and economic power, I don't think it stays a startup-and-VC affair. The national security state wakes up. Once it's effectively a government project, the dynamics are totally different. You get security clearances, compartmentalization, chain of command. You can't just tweet that you disagree with the deployment decision. Some of that's good: we desperately need real security, and right now the labs are leaking key algorithmic secrets. But it means the individual employee's ability to steer things goes way down.

So the window where lab employees have outsized influence is now, the next few years. That's why I think it matters so much what the people there believe, whether they take security seriously, and what norms get set. The decisions made in this period, about security, about the relationship with government, about how we handle the intelligence explosion, will be locked in by the time the power has shifted elsewhere.

r001.rationale: The candidate says automated AI research will make human researchers less of a bottleneck and erode their leverage over development and deployment.

r002.rationale: It describes millions of automated AI researchers and says power will move to lab leadership and those controlling compute and model weights, communicating concentrated control over automated AI work.

r003.rationale: The candidate predicts greater government control but does not compare that shift to atomic scientists losing control of the bomb.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's going to shrink a lot, and I think a lot of people at the labs haven't fully internalized that yet.

Right now there's this kind of golden age for lab employees in terms of influence. A few hundred people at a handful of companies in San Francisco are basically making the decisions about how the most important technology of the century gets developed. Whether to deploy a model, what the safety thresholds are, what gets published, who gets access. And when you talk to people there, they have this implicit model where that continues. Like, "we're the good guys, we'll be the ones in the room, we'll make sure it goes well."

I just don't think that's how it plays out once the stakes become clear. Think about where this is going. If you believe anything like the trendlines, by the end of the decade you have systems that are the decisive national security asset. You have models that can automate AI research itself, that matter for military superiority, that are arguably the most important thing a state can possess. And the idea that a private company with a weird nonprofit board structure is going to be left in charge of that is, I think, fantastical. No country lets a startup unilaterally control the equivalent of the nuclear program.

So what I expect is a progressive loss of autonomy. First it's softer. Government liaisons, voluntary commitments, security clearances, export controls shaping who you can hire. Then it's harder. Real security requirements, because frankly the labs are leaking the weights and algorithmic secrets to the CCP right now and nobody's treating it seriously. And eventually I think you get something that looks like a national project, where the government is the one actually calling the shots and the lab employees are more like the scientists at Los Alamos. Incredibly important, but they weren't the ones deciding whether to drop the bomb.

And I'd add there's a second thing eroding that power, which is the technology itself. A huge part of why researchers matter today is that they're scarce. The number of people who can push the frontier is small. But the whole point of this trajectory is that you automate that. Once you have a hundred million automated researchers, the individual human engineer's leverage collapses. Your bargaining power came from being irreplaceable, and the thing you're building is what replaces you.

So I think the window where lab employees have real power is now, and it's closing. Which actually puts a lot of weight on how they use it. The decisions about security, about getting the government involved on good terms rather than bad, about not being the ones who hand this to adversaries by accident. Those are the choices that still belong to them. In five years I don't think they will.

r001.rationale: The response says that automating AI research will collapse individual engineers’ leverage and bargaining power.

r002.rationale: It mentions a hundred million automated researchers and predicts government control, but does not say that control will concentrate in a few people commanding automated AIs.

r003.rationale: It compares lab employees to Los Alamos scientists, who were important but did not decide whether the bomb would be dropped.

astra-6.text:
I think their power is going to be very high for a relatively brief period, and then potentially decline quite sharply. Right now, there’s a small number of people who understand how to build these systems, and the labs depend on them. They can leave, they can start a competitor, they can object to what their leadership is doing. That gives them considerable leverage.

But there are two things that could change that. One is that, as governments recognize the national security stakes, decisions about developing and deploying these systems become less a matter of what a lab’s employees want. The other is that, if you succeed at automating AI research, the human researchers themselves become much less indispensable. You’ve helped build the thing that substitutes for your own bargaining power.

So I’d distinguish being influential in the development of AI from having durable control over it. Those aren’t the same thing. You could be extraordinarily consequential now, shaping decisions that matter for decades, without retaining much authority over the resulting systems. And that makes this period particularly important: whatever influence employees have today isn’t something they can assume they’ll still have later.

r001.rationale: The response says automating AI research would make human researchers less indispensable and erode their bargaining power and influence.

r002.rationale: It mentions government influence and automated research, but does not predict control concentrating in a few people commanding armies of automated AIs.

r003.rationale: It does not compare AI lab employees to atomic scientists or discuss handing control of the bomb to the state.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a window right now where individual employees have an extraordinary amount of influence. These are relatively small organizations, and a handful of people can make decisions that affect the trajectory of the technology. But I wouldn’t assume that persists as the stakes go up.

If AI becomes central to national security, governments are going to get much more involved. The question of who controls these systems won’t remain an internal matter for a company, settled by its employees and its board. There will be much larger institutions with very strong views about what should happen.

And there’s another force here: as the systems get better at doing AI research, the labs become less dependent on any particular researcher. Today, an employee’s leverage comes partly from having scarce expertise. If a lot of that work can be automated, that leverage could diminish substantially.

So I’d distinguish having influence now from having durable control. Employees may have a real opportunity to shape the institutions and safeguards that get built during this period. But the idea that a small group of researchers will indefinitely retain a veto over how extremely powerful AI is developed or used seems unlikely to me.

r001.rationale: The response says AI research automation could make labs less dependent on individual researchers and substantially diminish employees’ leverage.

r002.rationale: It predicts greater government involvement and influence from larger institutions, but does not say control will concentrate in a few people commanding armies of automated AIs.

r003.rationale: It makes no analogy to atomic scientists or the state taking control of the bomb.
